front: In Stein & Shah, what three creation/scale/synchronization goals do they state for threads?
back: Threads light enough to be created quickly, to exist by the thousands in one UNIX process, and to synchronize rapidly, while still giving fully concurrent access to system resources.

front: How is the LWP pool managed in Stein & Shah's library?
back: The library manages it; the pool grows or shrinks automatically so the process always makes progress without using excessive kernel resources. The programmer can also tune the thread/LWP relationship.

front: What is the paper's stated focus (per the Abstract)?
back: Scheduling and synchronizing user threads, and their interaction with UNIX signals, in a multiplexing threads library.

front: What are the two parts of the implementation described in the Introduction?
back: The threads library and a kernel modified to support multiple threads of control in one UNIX process (the kernel work is described in Eykholt 1992).

front: From outside a process, how visible are the number and identity of its threads?
back: Invisible. Threads are framed as execution resources applied to the problem at hand.

front: Beyond memory, what OS state do threads share, and is there protection between them?
back: They share most of the process's OS state, not only memory; e.g., a file opened by one thread can be read by another. There is no system-enforced protection between threads.

front: What four synchronization facilities does Stein & Shah's threads library provide?
back: Mutexes, condition variables, semaphores, and readers/writer locks (multiple readers, single writer).

front: In Stein & Shah's threads model, who allocates synchronization variables, and where?
back: The application, in ordinary memory.

front: How can threads in different processes synchronize, given they are invisible to each other?
back: Via synchronization variables placed in shared memory or mapped files; such variables must be marked process-shared at initialization.

front: Why might a synchronization variable have variants in Stein & Shah's model?
back: Variants can have different blocking behavior while keeping the same semantic (e.g., mutual exclusion).

front: What happens when any thread calls exit() in Stein & Shah's model?
back: It destroys all threads. (Each thread can otherwise make arbitrary system calls and interact with other processes normally, but some operations affect all threads.)

front: What does a per-thread signal mask let a thread do?
back: Block asynchronous signals while touching state that a signal handler also modifies.

front: Where does a synchronous signal (e.g., SIGSEGV) get delivered in Stein & Shah's model?
back: To the thread that caused it.

front: Where does an externally generated signal go in Stein & Shah's model?
back: To one thread that has the signal unmasked. If all threads mask it, it stays pending on the process until some thread unmasks it. Signals can also be sent to a particular thread in the same process.

front: In Stein & Shah's model, what scope do SIG_IGN and SIG_DFL have?
back: SIG_IGN discards received signals; SIG_DFL default actions (e.g., stop, continue, exit) apply to the whole process, not one thread.

front: Why did Stein & Shah reject per-thread signal handler vectors?
back: They add non-trivial storage per thread and permit conflicting requests (e.g., one thread SIG_DFL, another a handler), complicating implementation and use. Per-thread handling can be built on top of the shared vector if needed.

front: What are the two fork variants in Stein & Shah's model?
back: One clones the whole process with all its threads; the other reproduces only the calling thread (useful when the child will immediately call exec()).

front: How are threads implemented in terms of LWPs?
back: By a dynamically linked library on top of kernel-supported threads of control called LWPs.

front: What can each LWP do independently in Stein & Shah's architecture?
back: Each LWP is separately dispatched by the kernel, can make independent system calls, incur independent page faults, and run in parallel on a multiprocessor. All LWPs are scheduled by the kernel onto CPUs by scheduling class and priority.

front: What is the analogy between the library's scheduling and the kernel's scheduling?
back: The library schedules threads on its LWP pool the way the kernel schedules LWPs on processors.

front: Strictly, what does the SunOS 5.0 kernel schedule onto processors, and how do LWPs relate?
back: The kernel schedules kernel threads onto processors; kernel threads are the execution context underlying LWPs.

front: What are threads "simply" (per Stein & Shah), and what can the library do without OS involvement?
back: "Simply data structures and stacks" maintained by the library and unknown to the kernel. The library can switch an LWP between threads and create, destroy, block, or activate threads without OS involvement.

front: Why are LWPs much more expensive than threads in Stein & Shah?
back: Each LWP uses dedicated kernel resources; threads are just library data structures and stacks.

front: Why does Stein & Shah reject dedicating one LWP per thread, and which earlier package did that?
back: It would stop databases or window systems from using threads freely (e.g., one or more per client) or make them inefficient: a window system may be best written with many threads, but only a few need kernel resources at the same instant. CMU C Threads (Cooper 1990) used one LWP per thread.

front: In Stein & Shah, is a bound thread still a full thread with respect to synchronization?
back: Yes: a bound thread is still a thread and can synchronize with both bound and unbound threads in the process.

front: What does exposing both threads and LWPs separate, and how is LWP count framed?
back: It separates what the programmer sees (threads) from what the kernel provides (LWPs). Most programmers think only in threads and tune the relationship only when optimizing. LWP count is framed as the degree of real concurrency the application requires.

front: What does Figure 1 illustrate in Stein & Shah?
back: Two processes with threads above LWPs at the user/kernel boundary and LWPs mapped onto CPUs at the hardware level, showing different thread-to-LWP multiplexing per process.

front: What four attributes do LWPs have that threads lack?
back: A kernel-supported scheduling class, virtual-time timers, an alternate signal stack, and a profiling buffer. (LWPs share most process resources.)

front: Which existing LWP interfaces are Stein & Shah's LWP interfaces compatible with?
back: The UNIX International LWP interfaces of the time.

front: What does _lwp_create() do in Stein & Shah?
back: It creates another LWP in the process, starting from a machine context built by _lwp_makecontext().

front: What does _lwp_makecontext() build, and what does it buy?
back: A machine context emulating the standard calling sequence to a function; it is passed to _lwp_create(), giving some machine independence.

front: What kernel-provided LWP synchronization interfaces exist?
back: Mutexes, condition variables (wait, timed wait, signal, broadcast), and counting semaphores.

front: What priority-related protocols can LWP sync variants support?
back: Priority inversion prevention protocols such as priority inheritance.

front: Why are counting semaphores specifically provided among the LWP sync primitives?
back: So that a synchronization mechanism safe with respect to asynchronous signals is available.

front: When do LWP sync routines enter the kernel?
back: Only when they must; e.g., acquiring an uncontended LWP mutex may need no kernel entry. The kernel knows about LWP sync variables only during actual use.

front: Where do LWP sync variables live, and what does placing them in a mapped file enable?
back: In application memory; placed in shared memory or a mapped file they synchronize LWPs across all mapping processes. A mapped file lets the sync variables persist in the file, so a restarted application can keep using them without initialization.

front: How can processes synchronize on an LWP sync variable mapped at different virtual addresses?
back: A blocked LWP sleeps on a kernel sleep queue associated with the offset in the mapped file or segment. Internally a hash queue keyed by a two-word value: the vnode (internal file handle) and offset.

front: What do _lwp_getprivate()/_lwp_setprivate() provide, and what register holds it on SPARC?
back: One pointer's worth of LWP-private storage, typically used by a threads package to point to its thread structure. On SPARC this is register %g7.

front: Why can't ABI-compliant SPARC applications use %g7 for themselves?
back: %g7 is reserved to the system by the SPARC Application Binary Interface (USO 1990).

front: What alternative to a reserved register for LWP-private storage did Stein & Shah consider?
back: A private memory page per LWP. It costs more kernel effort and possibly more memory per LWP, but is probably best on register-constrained machines or where no user register is reserved to the system.

front: What is SIGLWP used for?
back: A new signal reserved for threads packages, used as an inter-LWP signal when directed at a particular LWP via _lwp_kill().

front: When is SIGWAITING generated and what do threads packages use it for?
back: Generated by the kernel when it detects that all LWPs in the process are blocked in indefinite waits. Threads packages use it to keep processes from deadlocking for lack of execution resources.

front: Which Figure 2 LWP interfaces suspend and resume a particular LWP, and how is the LWP named?
back: _lwp_suspend(lwpid) and _lwp_continue(lwpid), by LWP ID (lwpid_t, as returned by _lwp_self()).

front: Which Figure 2 LWP interfaces are the counting-semaphore operations?
back: _lwp_sema_wait(lwp_semap) and _lwp_sema_post(lwp_semap).

front: What earlier thread-ID scheme did Stein & Shah discard, and why?
back: An earlier implementation used a pointer to the thread structure as the ID; it was discarded in favor of an index into a table of pointers so the library can give meaningful errors when passed the ID of an exited, deallocated thread.

front: What is thread-local storage (TLS) in Stein & Shah, conceptually?
back: Thread-private storage in addition to the stack: conceptually unshared, statically allocated data for thread-private data needing fast access. Each thread has its own copy of thread-local variables while most program variables are shared.

front: How is TLS declared, and what are its initialization rules?
back: With a new #pragma unshared, supported by compiler and linker. TLS contents start zeroed; static initialization is not allowed.

front: How and when does the run-time linker compute TLS size, and what symbol does it define?
back: At program start, by summing the TLS segment sizes of all linked libraries and computing each item's offset; the linker defines _etls for the TLS size.

front: Why is TLS size computed at startup rather than link time?
back: So a library's TLS requirement is not compiled into the application binary and the library can change it without breaking the binary interface.

front: After startup, what restriction does fixed TLS size impose on dynamic linking?
back: TLS cannot grow, which restricts programmatic dynamic linking (dlopen()) to libraries without TLS.

front: Because of its restrictions, is TLS an exported interface, and what do applications get instead?
back: No, TLS is not exported; applications get POSIX thread-specific data (POSIX 1992) instead.

front: On SPARC, how does the compiler reference TLS and what register does it use?
back: The compiler assumes %g7 points to the TLS base (same register as the LWP private pointer) and emits %g7-relative TLS references; the library sets %g7 to the running thread's TLS base, with minimal scheduling impact.

front: How are LWPs in the pool set up, and what does a thread gain while executing?
back: LWPs are set up nearly identical so any thread can run on any of them; while executing, a thread is attached to an LWP and has all the attributes of a kernel-supported thread.

front: How are runnable unbound threads organized for dispatch?
back: All on a single user-level dispatch queue ordered by priority.

front: What is the range of thread priorities in Stein & Shah?
back: 0 to "infinity", where infinity is the maximum number representable in 32 bits.

front: Are thread priorities dynamic, and who can change them?
back: Fixed: the library never changes them dynamically as a time-shared discipline would. Only the thread itself or another thread in the same process can change them. An unbound thread's priority is used only by the user-level scheduler and is unknown to the kernel.

front: What does Figure 3 show about thread scheduling?
back: The LWP pool (with a minimum size and pool growth driven by SIGWAITING), the run queue, sleep queues on synchronization variables, and LWPs that are idle or switching between threads.

front: In Figure 3's discussion, what are the two states of an LWP in the pool?
back: Either idle or running a thread; an idle LWP waits on a synchronization variable for work (one of two possible, idling or parking).

front: When thread T1 becomes runnable, what happens to an idle LWP L1?
back: T1 goes on the dispatch queue; idle LWP L1 (if any) is awakened by signalling the idle synchronization variable, and L1 switches to the highest-priority thread on the queue.

front: If T1 blocks on a process-local sync object, what does its LWP L1 do?
back: L1 puts T1 on that object's sleep queue and switches to the highest-priority queued thread, or goes back to idling if the queue is empty.

front: If all LWPs are busy when T1 becomes runnable, what happens, and when does an LWP free up?
back: T1 waits on the dispatch queue. An LWP frees up when one is added to the pool or when a running thread blocks on a process-local sync variable, exits, or stops.

front: What are the five states of an unbound thread?
back: RUNNABLE, ACTIVE, SLEEPING, STOPPED, ZOMBIE.
source: Thread States and the Two Level Model

front: How do LWP states relate to the thread ACTIVE state?
back: While ACTIVE, the thread's LWP may be running on a processor, sleeping in the kernel, stopped, or waiting for a CPU on the kernel dispatch queue; the four LWP states refine the single thread ACTIVE state.
source: Thread States and the Two Level Model

front: In Figure 4, what are the thread state transitions on dispatch, preempt, sleep, and wakeup?
back: RUNNABLE to ACTIVE on dispatch; ACTIVE to RUNNABLE on preempt; ACTIVE to SLEEPING on sleep; SLEEPING to RUNNABLE on wakeup.

front: In Figure 4, what are the transitions for terminate, stop, and continue?
back: ACTIVE to ZOMBIE on terminate; stop from RUNNABLE, ACTIVE, or SLEEPING goes to STOPPED; continue from STOPPED goes to RUNNABLE.

front: What are the four LWP states within thread ACTIVE (Figure 5)?
back: RUNNING, BLOCKED, RUNNABLE, STOPPED.

front: In Figure 5, what are the LWP transitions for a blocking syscall, wakeup, dispatch, and timeslice/preempt?
back: RUNNING to BLOCKED on a blocking syscall; BLOCKED to RUNNABLE on wakeup; RUNNABLE to RUNNING on dispatch; RUNNING to RUNNABLE on timeslice or preempt (plus stop/continue to and from STOPPED).

front: What is "idling" in Stein & Shah?
back: When an unbound thread exits and no threads are RUNNABLE, its LWP switches to a small idle stack (one per LWP) and waits on a global LWP condition variable; when a thread becomes RUNNABLE the CV is signalled and an idle LWP wakes to run RUNNABLE threads.

front: What is "parking" in Stein & Shah?
back: When a bound thread blocks on a process-local sync variable, its LWP must stop too; it waits on an LWP semaphore associated with the thread. When the thread unblocks the parking semaphore is signalled and the LWP continues the thread.

front: What idling optimization applies when an unbound thread blocks with nothing else RUNNABLE?
back: Its LWP parks on the thread's semaphore instead of idling, avoiding a context switch to the idle stack and back if the thread becomes runnable quickly.

front: How do threads compete for LWPs, and what does the library do on preemption?
back: By priority, as kernel threads compete for CPUs. The library keeps a queue of ACTIVE threads; if a RUNNABLE thread may outrank some ACTIVE thread, the ACTIVE queue is searched, the victim removed and preempted from its LWP, and that LWP typically runs the higher-priority thread that caused the preemption.

front: What is the mechanism for preempting a thread?
back: Set a flag in the target's thread structure and send its LWP SIGLWP. The library always installs its own SIGLWP handler, which checks for a posted preemption, clears the flag, and switches to another thread.

front: What side effect does SIGLWP preemption have on a target blocked in a system call?
back: The call is interrupted by SIGLWP and restarted when the thread resumes; this matters only for calls that should not be restarted.

front: By default, who adjusts the number of LWPs used for unbound threads?
back: The library, automatically.
source: The Size of the LWP Pool

front: What is Requirement 1 for LWP pool sizing, with its example?
back: No deadlock for lack of LWPs. Example: more runnable unbound threads than LWPs while all active threads block in the kernel in indefinite waits (e.g., reading a tty); the process cannot progress until a waiter returns.
source: The Size of the LWP Pool

front: What is Requirement 2 for LWP pool sizing?
back: Efficient LWP use. One LWP per thread would leave many idle and overload the OS with resources for unused LWPs, losing the two-level model's advantages.
source: The Size of the LWP Pool

front: What is C in the pool-sizing discussion, and why doesn't the library match it exactly?
back: C is the number of ACTIVE plus RUNNABLE threads; it can fluctuate dramatically. If resizing were free, a pool equal to C always would satisfy both requirements; since resizing costs something, the library does not try to match C exactly.
source: The Size of the LWP Pool

front: Describe Stein & Shah's SIGWAITING protocol for growing the pool.
back: The library ignores SIGWAITING by default and installs a handler only when threads exceed LWPs. On SIGWAITING with runnable threads, it creates a new LWP and adds it to the pool. If no threads are runnable and threads are fewer than LWPs, it disables SIGWAITING.
source: The Size of the LWP Pool

front: What more aggressive pool-sizing alternative did Stein & Shah consider, and why not adopt it?
back: Compute a weighted time average of concurrency and adjust the pool more aggressively; not adopted because it is unknown whether the benefit outweighs the overhead of creating more LWPs.
source: The Size of the LWP Pool

front: Give Stein & Shah's two examples of thr_setconcurrency() values.
back: A multi-threaded file copy with one input and one output thread sets 2; a window system server sets expected simultaneously active clients times threads per client.
source: The Size of the LWP Pool

front: What is LWP aging, and what is the current timeout?
back: Earlier SIGWAITINGs or thr_setconcurrency() calls can leave more LWPs than threads, so LWPs unused for a "long" time (currently 5 minutes) are terminated. Implemented with a per-LWP timer set whenever the LWP starts idling; if it fires, the LWP terminates.
source: The Size of the LWP Pool

front: What does priocntl() do when a bound thread calls it, and what happens to unbound threads?
back: priocntl() (the system priority control interface) changes the LWP the thread is bound to and therefore the thread. Unbound threads keep being multiplexed normally in the presence of bound threads.

front: Where does a detached thread (bound or unbound) go when it exits?
back: On a single queue called deathrow with state ZOMBIE.

front: Why is freeing the stack deliberately not done at thread exit?
back: To make thread exit cheap by deferring unnecessary, expensive work.

front: What is the reaper frequency tradeoff tied to thread creation speed?
back: The reaper runs at high priority, so not too often; but not too rarely, because freed stacks go into a cache of available thread stacks that speeds stack allocation for new threads. Reaping rate thus affects thread creation speed.

front: What two basic types of synchronization variables does the library implement?
back: Process-local (the default) and process-shared.

front: Are the synchronization primitives safe to call from signal handlers?
back: Yes; the primitives are safe with respect to asynchronous signals and can be called from signal handlers.

front: What is the default blocking behavior of a process-local sync variable?
back: Put the thread to sleep. Each sync variable has its own sleep queue; the primitive puts the blocking thread there and surrenders the executing thread to the scheduler.

front: When blocking on a process-local sync variable, how do an unbound and a bound blocker differ?
back: Unbound: the scheduler dispatches another thread to its LWP. Bound: it must stay bound, so the LWP is parked on its thread.

front: On release of a process-local sync variable, how are bound vs unbound waiters handled?
back: The primitive checks for waiters and removes a blocked thread from the sleep queue. A bound thread is unparked so the kernel dispatches its LWP; an unbound thread is placed on the run queue for its priority and then dispatched to an LWP in priority order.

front: What are process-shared synchronization objects for?
back: Placed in memory accessible to more than one process to synchronize threads in different processes.

front: Why must process-shared sync variables be initialized at creation?
back: Their blocking behavior differs from the default; each primitive has an initialization function that marks the variable process-shared, letting the primitives recognize it and block correctly.

front: How do process-shared primitives achieve cross-process synchronization?
back: They rely on the LWP synchronization primitives: blocked threads sleep in the kernel still attached to their LWPs, and the LWP primitives handle cross-process synchronization.

front: What is the core difficulty of signals in a two-level model?
back: Providing SunOS MT signal semantics where the kernel sends signals but cannot see user threads or their masks, so it cannot make correct delivery decisions by itself.

front: What does "async safe" mean, and what additional signal goal does Stein & Shah state?
back: A function is async safe if it is reentrant with respect to signals, i.e., callable from an asynchronously invoked signal handler. The additional goal is cheap async-safe synchronization primitives.

front: Why do cheap async-safe primitives matter per Stein & Shah?
back: For multi-threaded libraries with internal critical sections, such as the threads library and its clients like libc.

front: Give Stein & Shah's mutex_lock() deadlock example and its fix.
back: mutex_lock() is interrupted while holding internal threads-library lock L; the handler calls mutex_lock(), tries to take L again, and deadlocks. Masking signals during L's critical section fixes it, so efficient signal masking was a goal (it yields efficient async-safe critical sections).

front: What signal-model strategy did Stein & Shah reject, where each LWP mirrors its thread's mask?
back: Each LWP mirrors its current thread's signal mask, letting the kernel choose directly among ACTIVE threads; the set of receivable signals then changes as threads cycle through ACTIVE.

front: What two problems does the rejected mask-mirroring strategy have?
back: A rarely ACTIVE thread that is the only one with some signal enabled effectively sleeps waiting for a signal it never receives; and a system call is needed whenever an LWP switches between threads with different masks or an active thread changes its mask.

front: In the adopted signal design, what set of signals can the process receive?
back: The intersection of all thread signal masks (in mask terms, a signal is blocked only if every thread blocks it). The library keeps each LWP mask equal to or less restrictive than its thread's mask, so the kernel occasionally delivers signals to ACTIVE threads that have them disabled.

front: If the global signal handler finds the signal masked, what does it do?
back: It sets the current LWP's mask to the current thread's mask, then resends the signal: to the process if undirected, to that LWP if directed. The kernel's delivery information lets it distinguish directed from undirected.

front: What is the basic means by which thr_kill() sends a signal to another thread?
back: Send it to the LWP the thread runs on.

front: How does thr_kill() behave if the target thread is not ACTIVE?
back: It posts the signal in the thread's pending-signals mask; the thread receives pending signals when it resumes, because the context-switch code sends them to the LWP that resumes the thread.

front: How does thr_kill() behave if the target thread is ACTIVE but its LWP blocks the signal?
back: It sends the signal to the LWP via lwp_kill(). If the LWP blocks it (implying the thread does too), the signal stays pending on the LWP until the thread unblocks it, and meanwhile the thread is temporarily bound to that LWP until delivery.

front: What is thr_sigsetmask(), and what does it cost when no signals occur?
back: The interface for masking signals during critical sections; if no signals occur it makes no system call and costs about as much as writing the user-level thread mask.

front: What even faster path does the library use for its own critical sections?
back: It sets/clears a special flag in the thread structure on entry/exit, acting as a mask-all-signals bit; if the flag is set when a signal arrives, the global handler defers the signal as in the mask-mismatch case.

front: Why is the kernel's standard /proc debugging interface insufficient for library-supported threads?
back: The debugger needs information about threads inside the process, which /proc does not provide.

front: What debugging approach did Stein & Shah reject, and why?
back: Building full knowledge of the threads implementation into the debugger, which would force a debugger re-release whenever internal library data structures change.

front: What debugging design did Stein & Shah adopt?
back: A separate dynamically linked thread debugging library, loaded via dlopen(), holding all threads-library-specific knowledge; it lets the debugger enumerate threads and get/set the state and registers of each thread, ACTIVE or not.

front: What does the thread-extended DBX do with the debugging library?
back: It lists all threads and their states (sleeping, running, active, stopped, zombied) and can switch focus to any thread so standard DBX commands inspect its state.
